paras.text: Nitin Nohria, Boris Groysberg and Linda-Eling Lee examine current research into what motivates employees, and report on their own research in this area

Getting people to do their best work, even in trying circumstances, is one of a manager's most enduring challenges. Indeed, deciphering what motivates us as human beings is a centuries-old puzzle. Some of history's most influential thinkers about human behavior among them Aristotle in the ancient world and Sigmund Freud in the early 20th century have struggled to understand its nuances and have taught us a tremendous amount about why people do the things they do. Some philosophers, however, didn't have the advantage of knowledge gleaned from modern brain science. Imagine trying to infer how a car works by examining its movements (starting, stopping, accelerating, turning) without being able to take apart the engine.

Fortunately, new cross-disciplinary research in fields like neuroscience, biology and evolutionary psychology has allowed us to learn more about the human brain. Our synthesis of this research suggests that people are guided by four basic emotional needs, or drives, that are the product of our common evolutionary heritage. These are the drives to acquire, bond, comprehend, and defend. Because these four drives are hardwired into our brains, the degree to which they are satisfied directly affects our emotions and, by extension, our behavior. Let's look at how each one operates.

The drive to acquire. We are all driven to acquire goods that bolster our sense of well-being. We experience delight when this drive is fulfilled, discontentment when it is thwarted. This phenomenon applies not only to physical goods like clothing, housing and money, but also to events that improve social status, such as being promoted. The drive to acquire tends to be relative (we always compare what we have with what others possess) and insatiable (we always want more). That explains why people always care not just about their own compensation packages but about others' as well.

The drive to bond. Many animals bond with their parents, kinship group, or tribe, but only humans extend that connection to larger collectives such as organizations and nations. When fulfilled, this drive is associated with strong positive emotions like love and caring and, when not, with negative ones like loneliness. At work, the drive to bond accounts for the enormous boost in motivation when employees feel proud of belonging to the organization, and for their loss of morale when the institution betrays them. It also explains why employees find it hard to break out of a work group: people become attached to their closest co-workers.

The drive to comprehend. We want very much to make sense of the world around us, to produce theories that make events comprehensible. We are frustrated when things seem senseless, and we are invigorated by the challenge of working out answers. In the workplace, the drive to comprehend accounts for the desire to make a meaningful contribution. Employees are motivated by jobs that challenge them and enable them to grow and learn, and they are demoralized by those that seem to be monotonous or lead to a dead end. Talented employees who feel trapped often leave their companies to find new challenges elsewhere.

The drive to defend. We all naturally defend ourselves, our property, our family and friends and our ideas and beliefs against external threats. This drive is rooted in the basic fight-or-flight response common to most animals. In humans, it manifests itself not just as aggressive or defensive behavior, but also as a quest to create institutions that promote justice and that allow people to express their own thoughts and beliefs. The drive to defend tells us a lot about people's resistance to change; it's one reason employees can be distressed by the prospect of their company being taken over, even if the deal represents the only hope for an organization's survival.

So what actions can managers take to satisfy the four drives and, thereby, increase their employees' overall motivation? We recently completed two major studies to evaluate the importance of these drives in terms of employee motivation. In one, we surveyed 385 employees of two global businesses. In the other, we surveyed employees from 300 successful local companies. To define overall motivation, we focused on four commonly measured workplace indicators: effort, satisfaction, commitment and intention to quit.

Both studies showed that certain drives influence some motivational indicators more than others. Fulfilling the drive to bond has the greatest effect on employee commitment, for example, whereas meeting the drive to comprehend is most closely linked with employee effort. The drive to acquire is most easily satisfied by an organization's reward system. A clear example of this can be found in the merger of two large companies, HBES and Phillips Quartermain. When HBES acquired Phillips Quartermain, it inherited a company in which the reward system was dominated by politics and status. HBES introduced a new system that held managers responsible for specific goals and rewarded good performance over average performance. Former Phillips Quartermain employees embraced their new company to an unusual extent in the aftermath of an acquisition in part because the reward system was tough but recognized individual achievement. The most effective way to fulfill the drive to bond is to create a culture that promotes teamwork, openness and friendship. HBES broke through Phillips Quartermain's mentality by bringing together people from the two firms to work on well-defined cost savings. The new culture encouraged people to break old attachments and form new bonds.

But a company can best improve overall motivational scores by satisfying all four drives in concert. Each of the four drives is independent; they cannot be ordered hierarchically or substituted one for another. You can't just pay your employees a lot and hope they'll feel enthusiastic about their work in an organization where bonding is not fostered. To fully motivate your employees, you must address all four drives.
